```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5)
library(meddecide)
```

This article is a short introduction to ROC analysis with **Advanced ROC
Analysis** (`psychopdaROC()`, **meddecide > ROC**). For every option see the
[comprehensive guide](meddecide-psychopdaroc-comprehensive.html); for a
clinically oriented alternative see
[Clinical ROC Analysis](meddecide-enhancedroc-comprehensive.html).

## Data

```{r data}
df_roc <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "roc_example.csv", package = "meddecide"))
table(df_roc$class)
```

## ROC curve and AUC

Columns are passed by name. Name both the positive and the negative level of the
outcome: they are required, and the analysis waits until both are chosen rather
than guessing which level means "disease".

```{r roc}
roc_res <- psychopdaROC(
  data = df_roc,
  dependentVars = "value",   # marker column(s)
  classVar = "class",        # outcome column
  positiveClass = "pos",
  negativeClass = "neg",
  plotROC = TRUE
)

roc_res$resultsTable[[1]]$asDF  # optimal cut-point, sensitivity, specificity, AUC
roc_res$aucSummaryTable$asDF    # AUC with its confidence interval
roc_res$plotROC[[1]]            # ROC curve
```

`resultsTable` and `plotROC` hold one element per marker, hence `[[1]]`.

By default the cut-point maximises Youden's J (sensitivity + specificity - 1)
and the AUC confidence interval uses DeLong's standard error on the logit scale
(`aucInference = "logit"`). With 20 cases, as here,
the interval is wide and the "optimal" cut-point is unstable; a cut-point chosen
on the same data looks better than it will on new patients.

## Choosing a threshold

- **Youden's J** balances sensitivity and specificity. It ignores prevalence and
  the different costs of false positives and false negatives.

For a marker that is higher in disease:

- **Rule-out**: pick the highest threshold that still gives the required
  sensitivity (for example at least 0.95).
- **Rule-in**: pick the lowest threshold that gives the required specificity.
- **Consequences**: when the harms of the two errors differ, use a cost ratio
  (`method = "oc_cost_ratio"`) or a decision curve (`decisioncurve()`,
  **meddecide > Decision Curve Analysis**).

`sensSpecTable = TRUE` adds a confusion matrix at the chosen cut-point, and
`fixedSensSpecAnalysis = TRUE` reports the threshold that achieves a fixed
sensitivity or specificity.
